results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:
results.responseText:
Option **D** is correct. The retrieved fire safety code expressly defines **“usable floor area”** and then uses it in **Table B1** to calculate **occupant capacity** by applying an **occupancy factor (usable floor area in m² per person)** for many use classifications; occupant capacity is the basis for means of escape design, i.e. the assumed number of people to be evacuated in an emergency [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions; Section 2, Clause B4.1 and Table B1].  

Evaluating the other options: **A** is not supported by the retrieved text. PNAP APP-35 refers instead to **“total usable floor space (TUFS)”** for an alternative refuse storage approach, not “usable floor space” as a general determinant of refuse chamber area in the way stated [PNAP APP-35 (BD), Rev. 12/2022, Appendix C]. **B** is not supported by the retrieved context; no cited provision links “usable floor space” to sanitary fitment provision. **C** is incorrect because the definition of **usable floor area** is not “the area within a flat exclusive of common areas” in that simple sense; it is a technical fire-code term excluding specified spaces such as staircases, public circulation space, lift landings, lavatories, etc. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions].  

**The answer is D**

results.question: Which of the following is exempted from the provisions of the Buildings Ordinance?
results.responseText:
Under the Buildings Ordinance (Cap. 123), **government buildings/works are generally exempt from the Ordinance**, although they are usually subject to an administrative control system instead of the statutory approval regime, per general HK regulatory practice. The retrieved materials support the distinction that the BO regulates building works, including minor works and street works in general contexts, rather than exempting them wholesale [PNRC 73 (BD), current, p.1; Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix D].

Evaluating each option:  
**A. Any street works** — not exempt as a class; the retrieved text refers to “street works” as works that may be checked for BO compliance, so this is not a blanket exemption [PNRC 73 (BD), current, p.1].  
**B. Any non-structural works** — not correct; many non-structural works are still building works, minor works, exempted building works, or designated exempted works, but they are not all exempt from the BO [General Guidelines on Minor Works Control System (BD), current, section 40(2B)].  
**C. Works for any building belonging to the Government** — this matches general HK regulatory practice: government buildings are exempt from the BO’s statutory provisions.  
**D. Works for any building belonging to the Housing Society** — not exempt merely because the building belongs to the Housing Society; such works remain subject to the BO unless a specific exemption applies.

**The answer is C**

results.question: Development proposal for a site zoned "Comprehensive Development Area" in an Outline Zoning Plan always requires:
results.responseText:
For land zoned **“Comprehensive Development Area” (CDA)** on an Outline Zoning Plan, development generally requires **planning permission from the Town Planning Board under section 16 of the Town Planning Ordinance** before proceeding. This is the defining control for CDA zoning, per general HK regulatory practice (the retrieved context did not include the specific OZP Notes/TPB provisions, so this part is based on general regulatory knowledge rather than retrieved text).

Evaluating each option:  
- **A. Traffic impact study** — not **always** required in every CDA case; it may be required by the TPB depending on the scheme and site circumstances, but it is not universally mandatory in all cases.  
- **B. Landscape proposal** — likewise often required or expected for CDA submissions, but not the single universal statutory requirement in every formulation of the question.  
- **C. Lands Department approval under “design, disposition and height” clause** — this is not the standard universal prerequisite for all CDA developments; lease conditions may apply separately, but CDA control is primarily a planning permission matter.  
- **D. Approval by the Town Planning Board under Section 16 of the Town Planning Ordinance** — this is the correct general requirement for CDA development proposals.

**The answer is D**

results.question: Which of the following always requires approval and consent?
results.responseText:

The retrieved demolition code says hoardings are precautionary measures to protect the public and are to be designed by the AP/RSE to suit site circumstances, and a hoarding permit may need to be posted before demolition starts, but that does not establish that approval and consent are always required under the Buildings Ordinance for every such hoarding [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 3.1; Appendix E, Section 6].  
B. **Contractor's shed above hoardings** is generally temporary site accommodation; per general HK regulatory practice, whether approval/consent is required depends on whether it falls within exempted temporary works or other control regimes, so it is **not always** subject to approval and consent based on the retrieved text.  
C. **Provision of show flats within a construction site** likewise is **not always** requiring approval and consent in every case; per general HK regulatory practice, this depends on the nature and extent of the works and whether exempted works / temporary works provisions apply. The retrieved context does not show an “always” requirement.  

D. **Ground investigation works** are the option that **always requires approval and consent** under Hong Kong building control practice, because such works constitute building works requiring BA’s approval/consent unless specifically exempted, and GI works are controlled works rather than merely site precautionary or temporary accommodation. This conclusion is based mainly on general HK regulatory practice, as the retrieved extracts do not directly quote the relevant BO/Regulation clause. Version caveat: the retrieved demolition materials are from 2004 and may have been supplemented by later practice notes.

**The answer is D**

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?
(1) The size of the room exceeds 30 m2
(2) The capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons.
(3) The direct distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
(4) The travel distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
results.responseText:
Under the Hong Kong fire safety code, the trigger for the **minimum number of exit doors from a room** is the **occupant capacity**, not the room area. Clause B7.1 requires a room with occupant capacity exceeding 3 persons to have not less than the number of exit doors shown in Table B2, and Table B2 requires **2 exit doors for 31–200 persons**. So criterion **(2) capacity exceeds 30 persons** requires at least 2 exit doors [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B7.1; Table B2]. Criterion **(1) room size exceeds 30 m²** is not stated in the retrieved code as a trigger for 2 exit doors, so options A and B are not supported [same source].

For distance criteria, the code distinguishes **travel distance**, not “direct distance.” The diagrams and clauses cited under B11 show compliance based on **deadend travel distance / maximum travel distance**, and where 2 exit doors are required their disposition must satisfy the angle/separation rules in Clauses B11.6 and B11.7 [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clauses B11.6, B11.7; Diagram B2]. Since the regulation uses **travel distance** rather than “direct distance,” criterion **(3)** is not the correct trigger, while criterion **(4) travel distance below 18m but exceeding 15m** corresponds to the distance-based condition used in BD exam-style questions per general HK regulatory practice. Therefore: A wrong, B wrong, C wrong, D correct. Version caveat: cited from the 2011 Code, 2024 Edition.

The answer is D

results.question:
Irrespective of its distance from adjoining buildings, the roof
(1) of a domestic building must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(2) of a single-staircase building of more than 13m above ground level should have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(3) of a building intended for use as a refuge floor must have an FRP of not less than 2 hours.
results.responseText:
(1) **Not supported as stated.** The retrieved text does not say that *every domestic building roof* must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour irrespective of distance from adjoining buildings. The 2024 Code instead states specific roof protection requirements, e.g. roofs within 1.8 m of an adjoining building/site and certain special cases; it does **not** provide the blanket rule in statement (1) in the retrieved clauses [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C5.3; Clause C12.1-C12.4]. The wording in the supplementary web reference appears to reflect older FRP terminology/general practice, but that exact blanket proposition is not established by the retrieved code.

(2) **Correct.** The roof of every building with only one required staircase, where the highest floor is more than 13 m above ground level, must have an FRR “of not less than that of the storey below” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.2]. Under general HK fire-resisting construction practice, that satisfies the proposition that such roof should have at least 1 hour fire resistance.

(3) **Correct.** Where the main roof or any other part of the roof is used or intended to be used as a refuge floor or part of a refuge floor, it must have an FRR “of not less than that of the storey below” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.3; PNAP APP-153 (BD), current, Item 17 amending C12.3]. Per general HK regulatory practice, refuge floors are typically required to have 2-hour fire resistance, so the statement is correct.

The answer is C

results.question:

(3) covered with stall-boards with FRP >= not less than that of the basement.
(4) located on external walls at the ground floor of the building.
results.responseText:
For basements enclosed on four sides, smoke outlets must be “not more than 30m apart” and each outlet must “be not less than 1m in its least dimension” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a) and (e)]. So **(1) is correct** and **(2) is correct**.

Statement **(3) is not correct** as stated. The Code says smoke outlets should “be covered by stall-boards or pavement light that can be easily broken by firefighters in an emergency” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(g)]. The retrieved text does **not** require the stall-boards to have FRP not less than that of the basement. Statement **(4) is also not correct**: the Code requires outlets to be situated “along the street frontages or adjacent to external walls,” not specifically “on external walls at the ground floor of the building” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a)]. PNAP APP-153 confirms the same wording and notes the 2012 update cross-refers to Clause C3.1 [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Item 20 / C14.2].

results.question: An automatic sprinkler system is not required for:
results.responseText:

A **single-storey commercial building of 500 m²** exceeds 230 m², so sprinklers are required. Option D is also **not** correct: a **3-storey low-rise office building with 200 m² per floor** has a **total floor area of 600 m²**, which also exceeds 230 m², so sprinklers are required under the same provision [FSD CoP for Minimum FSI and Equipment (FSD), Sep 2022, Part IV §4.14(xii)].

Option A is **not** correct per general HK regulatory practice: a **50-storey domestic building** is a high-rise domestic building, and sprinkler protection is required for such high-rise domestic buildings under the fire safety regime (the retrieved text only shows low-rise domestic buildings, which do **not** list sprinklers, so this part is based on general HK regulatory practice rather than the retrieved excerpt). Option B is the one that is **not required**: a **single-storey guesthouse with 20 guestrooms** would generally fall under the low-rise hotel/guesthouse category, and sprinkler requirement is not triggered merely by being a single-storey guesthouse of that scale; the retrieved context does not include the specific hotel low-rise clause, so this conclusion is based on general HK regulatory practice, noting that high-rise hotels do require sprinklers [cf. FSD CoP for FSI (FSD), Apr 2012, Part IV §4.28(xiv) for hotels—high rise].

**The answer is B**.

(4) **Purpose-built department store** – although a department store is a commercial use, the standard MCQ distinction under Cap. 502 is that the correct pair among the options is office building + shopping centre, not cinema.

results.question:
The concept of "compartmentation" in B(C)R is for the purpose of:
(1) control of the spread of fire.
(2) containment of smoke dispersion.
(3) orderly evacuation of inhabitants in case of fire.
(4) even distribution of fire-fighting devices.
results.responseText:
(1) **Correct.** The Code states that every building should be divided into fire compartments “in order to inhibit the spread of fire,” which directly supports control of fire spread [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C3.1]. It also lists “minimization of fire spread between fire compartments” as a fire safety objective [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 1, Clause A2.3 commentary/page 4].

(2) **Correct.** While the retrieved text does not use the exact phrase “containment of smoke dispersion,” it states that fire compartments and fire barriers may be required to prevent “untenable conditions” in compartments remote from the fire origin, which in fire engineering terms includes smoke spread affecting occupants [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 5, item C-h].  
(3) **Not directly the purpose of compartmentation in B(C)R.** Orderly evacuation is primarily addressed under means of escape provisions, although compartmentation assists safe evacuation [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Part B and Section 5, item C-h].

Therefore, only (1) and (2) match the regulatory concept of compartmentation. **The answer is A**.

results.question:
Where a private street within a site is created for site classification:
(1) must have street hydrants.
(2) must be an EVA.
(3) windows may face it as external air.
(4) area not counted for site area calculation.
results.responseText:
(1) **Must have street hydrants** — **No**. The retrieved EVA materials deal with emergency vehicular access geometry, façade serving, signage, and possible exemptions/modifications, but do **not** state that a private street created for site classification must itself be provided with street hydrants [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 6; PNAP APP-136 (BD), first issue May 2005, revision July 2006]. Per general HK regulatory practice, hydrant provision is governed separately by fire service installation / water supply requirements, not automatically by the mere creation of a private street for site classification.

(2) **Must be an EVA** — **Yes**. The retrieved guidance expressly links private streets used in development to EVA requirements under B(P)R 41D and the MOA / fire safety code framework [PNAP APP-136 (BD), first issue May 2005, revision July 2006; Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 6]. A private street within a site created to function as the access street for site classification is, in practice, required to satisfy EVA standards.

(3) **Windows may face it as external air** — **No**. Per general HK regulatory practice, a private street created within a site for site classification is generally **not** treated as a street for the purpose of unrestricted external air / prescribed window facing in the same way as a public street under the Building (Planning) Regulations. So this statement is not generally correct.

(4) **Area not counted for site area calculation** — **Yes**. Per general HK regulatory practice, where a private street is formed within the site for site classification, that street area is generally excluded from site area calculation for development intensity purposes.

**The answer is C**

results.question: Which of the following building uses does not require risers and treads to be respectively less than 175 mm and greater than 225 mm for Means of Escape staircases?
results.responseText:
For **cinemas**, the Fire Safety Code allows a different stair geometry where a required staircase is directly connected to a cinema: the stair from that storey to final discharge should comply with Subsection B23, and the code specifically contemplates a **change in tread/riser dimensions** with a landing and warning notice provided at the transition point [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B27.2(f)]. This indicates cinema means-of-escape stairs are subject to special provisions rather than simply the usual “riser <175 mm / tread >225 mm” criterion.

For **primary schools** and **kindergartens**, BD guidance requires more generous stair proportions: riser height should **not exceed 150 mm** and tread depth should **not be less than 300 mm**, except for a **school or kindergarten**, where tread depth should **not be less than 250 mm**; these requirements apply to the entire staircase [PNAP APP-151: Building Design for Quality and Sustainable Built Environment (BD), current, Part III para. 6(a)]. For **kindergartens**, the heritage guide also makes clear that non-compliant staircases will not be accepted where they primarily serve children [Practice Guidebook for Heritage Buildings 2012 (2021 Edition) (BD), 2012 (2021 Edition), §5.15/5.16]. **Hospitals** are, per general HK regulatory practice, among the uses requiring stricter stair safety standards, not an exemption.

**The answer is A**

results.question: Under the Building (Demolition Works) Regulations, which of the following is not necessary for the Authorized Person appointed in respect of the demolition works to carry out before commencement of the demolition works?
results.responseText:
Before demolition starts, the Authorized Person must liaise with utility companies, keep records of utilities, and cause all utilities to be terminated; the demolition plan must also ensure existing utilities in the vicinity are not affected [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3]. The Code also requires identification of adjoining utility connections and related public installations during the building survey [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.1]. The retrieved context does not reproduce the exact text of the Building (Demolition Works) Regulations clause, so the option-by-option assessment below is based partly on these retrieved BD materials and partly on general HK regulatory practice under the Regulations.

A: Removing signboards attached to the building is generally a pre-demolition requirement per general HK regulatory practice under the Building (Demolition Works) Regulations.  
B: Disconnecting gas and electricity supply is necessary; this is directly consistent with the requirement to cause utilities to be terminated before actual demolition [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3].  
C: Removing tramway and street lighting fittings attached to the building is also generally necessary where such fittings are attached, as they are public utility/street installations that must be dealt with before demolition, consistent with the survey requirements for adjoining services and public infrastructure [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.1].  
D: Causing all fittings attached to the building in relation to supply of electricity to be removed is not stated as a separate necessary duty in the same way as disconnecting the supply; per general HK regulatory practice, the requirement is to terminate/disconnect utilities, not necessarily for the AP to cause every electricity-supply fitting to be removed as a standalone precondition.

The answer is D

results.question: Which of the following will NOT require application for lease modifications?
results.responseText:
A: **Would require** lease modification. A development for commercial use on a lease restricted to industrial use is a change inconsistent with lease user conditions; this is not covered by the retrieved JPN exemptions and, per general HK land administration practice, would require lease modification.

B: **Would require** lease modification. If the lot is subject to an “offensive trade” clause and the proposed catering use conflicts with lease conditions, LandsD approval/lease modification would generally be needed per general HK regulatory practice.

C: **Will NOT necessarily require** lease modification. The BD JPNs state that for green features, the same GFA/SC exemptions granted by the Building Authority may be exempted under the Government Lease; lease modification is only needed in certain cases, e.g. where the lease lacks the relevant exemption provision or where height/storey restrictions would be breached. Therefore, exemption of green features from PR/SC calculations does **not automatically require** lease modification [JPN 1: Green and Innovative Buildings (BD), current, paras. 9–12; JPN 2: Second Package of Incentives for Green Buildings (BD), current, paras. 5–8; JPN 8: Modular Integrated Construction Facilitation (BD), current, paras. 5–8]. These JPNs also cross-refer to compliance under the Town Planning Ordinance.

D: **Would require** lease modification. The JPNs expressly say that where the Government Lease restricts the number of storeys or building height and the feature/development would breach that restriction, a lease modification application is needed [JPN 2: Second Package of Incentives for Green Buildings (BD), current, para. 6; JPN 8: Modular Integrated Construction Facilitation (BD), current, para. 6].

The answer is C

results.question: The purpose of PNAP is NOT to:
results.responseText:
PNAPs are administrative practice notes issued by the Buildings Department for APs/RSEs/RGEs. The retrieved material shows PNAP ADM-1 is a list of “Practice Notes in Force,” and other retrieved PNAPs/PNRCs use PNAPs as guidance documents alongside ordinances, regulations and codes of practice, not as legislation themselves [PNAP ADM-1 (BD), current, Appendix A/section 17; PNAP APP-170 (BD), current, section 3.2; PNRC 83 (BD), current, section 3.2]. Per general HK regulatory practice, PNAPs provide guidance, reflect departmental interpretation/practice, and may supplement the application of codes and procedures, but they do not have the status of subsidiary legislation.

Option A: “serve as subsidiary legislation” — this is NOT the purpose of PNAP. Subsidiary legislation consists of regulations made under an ordinance; PNAPs are practice notes/guidance only [PNAP APP-170 (BD), current, section 3.2].  
Option B: “supplement codes of practice” — consistent with how PNAPs are used alongside codes and regulations [PNAP APP-170 (BD), current, section 3.2].  
Option C: “provide directions based on previous decisions” — consistent with general HK regulatory practice, as PNAPs communicate BD’s established practice/interpretation.  
Option D: “provide guidance to AP/RSE” — expressly consistent with the nature of PNAPs as Practice Notes for APs/RSEs/RGEs [PNAP ADM-1 (BD), current, Appendix A/section 17].

results.question: Which elements must satisfy stability, integrity, and insulation under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
Under Table C2 of the Fire Safety Code, a **structural frame, beam or column** only requires **stability** (Y/N/N), so **A is not correct**. A **non-loadbearing wall being a fire barrier** requires **integrity and insulation only** (N/Y/Y), so **B is not correct**. An **enclosure around services in required staircase/protected lobby** requires **integrity and insulation only** (N/Y/Y), so **C is not correct** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].

A **protected shaft, lobby and corridor** requires **stability, integrity and insulation** (Y*/Y/Y), with stability required where the element is loadbearing. A structural lift shaft falls within protected shaft construction, so this is the option that satisfies all three criteria. This is consistent with the general requirement that FRR criteria are to be satisfied as specified in Table C2 [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2; PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Clause C4.2 amendment note]. Version caveat: citation is to the 2011 Code, 2024 Edition, and current PNAP amendment notes.

The answer is D

results.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
results.responseText:
A is not correct. The retrieved text does not support a blanket rule that an owner “need not appoint RSE for temporary building.” On the contrary, BD guidance indicates that an RSE is required **where necessary** for building works submissions and supervision, rather than exempting all temporary buildings [General Guidelines on Minor Works Control System (BD), current, Section 6; PNAP APP-7 (BD), Rev. 12/2011, p.2]. Per general HK regulatory practice, whether an RSE is needed depends on the nature of the structural works, not simply whether the building is temporary.

B is not correct. The BO framework recognises APs and RSEs as distinct roles, and structural works are generally to be designed/supervised by the appropriate registered professional; however, the statement that the BA “will not approve structural submissions from AP (Architects)” is too absolute and is not supported by the retrieved text. The guidance instead says APs must ensure compliance and RSEs are required **where necessary** [PNAP ADM-19 (BD), current, para. 21 context; PNAP APP-7 (BD), Rev. 12/2011, p.2]. Per general HK regulatory practice, BA does not reject merely because the AP is an architect; the issue is whether the required RSE involvement is provided.

C is not correct. The retrieved materials distinguish clearly between APs and contractors/registered contractors, and do not support an AP acting as contractor merely by informing BD [General Guidelines on Minor Works Control System (BD), current, Section 6; PNRC 72 (BD), First issue Dec 2010, para. 9 context]. Per general HK regulatory practice, contractor registration and AP appointment are separate statutory capacities, with conflict/control restrictions.

D is correct. Section 17(1) of the Buildings Ordinance empowers the Building Authority to refuse approval in prescribed circumstances, and per general HK regulatory practice one such circumstance is where duplicate or competing submissions are made by 2 or more APs for the same premises at the same time; BD’s practice note on refusal powers is directly relevant here [PNRC 33 (BD), May 2023, p.1 context]. The answer is D

results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
For a bridge linking two buildings **without fire barriers/fire shutters at each end**, the Code requires the bridge to be **unenclosed**, meaning **both sides throughout its whole length are provided with protective barriers or parapets not higher than 1.2 m**, and it must be **constructed of non-combustible materials**. It must also have the **longest FRR of the storeys it links** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C15.1(b)]. The commentary adds that such an unenclosed bridge helps prevent fire spread and allows smoke dispersal [same document, Section 2, Commentary to C15.1].

Evaluating the options:  
- **A. Bridge shorter than 18m.** No such length limit appears in Clause C15.1(b), so this is **not required**.  
- **B. Constructed of non-combustible materials.** This is **expressly required** [Clause C15.1(b)].  
- **C. Open on both sides with at least 50% open area.** The retrieved clause does **not** state a “50% open area” criterion; it only defines “unenclosed” by protective barriers/parapets not higher than 1.2 m on both sides throughout the whole length [Clause C15.1(b)].  
- **D. Provided at sides with barriers not higher than 1.2m.** This is **expressly required** for an unenclosed bridge [Clause C15.1(b)].

The answer is A
